title: Our voice, our world
grammar: Discourse markers for debating (having said that, on balance, all in all)

scene.speaker: nova
scene.bubble: The final debate of the year! Let's use everything we've learned — grammar and courage together — to make our voices heard.
scene.intro: Welcome to the last unit of B2 First, Grade Ten. The Inspiring Nordic — Trades project closes with Sofía, Mateo, Liam and Nadia holding a formal class debate, and this unit gets you ready for it. You will learn discourse markers for debating — having said that, on balance, all in all, to be honest, the way I see it — and see how this year's grammar, mixed conditionals, the causative and relative clauses, can make an argument sound more convincing. You will read five short opinions in the format of Reading Part 7, listen to an interview about the debate in the format of Listening Part 4, complete a word formation task and key word transformations, and write a review of a debate, a talk or a podcast. One year of English, one voice. Let's use it well.

activities.title: Speaking — Parts 1 and 2. Talk with a partner, then record yourself.

tips.expect: Part 1 (2 minutes): the examiner asks you and your partner questions about yourselves — studies, opinions, free time. Part 2 (about 4 minutes): you talk alone for 1 minute about two of three photographs, answering the question printed above them; then your partner answers a brief question about your photographs (about 30 seconds).
how: In Part 1, give a reason or an example, not just a one-word answer — but do not turn it into a speech.
In Part 2, do not simply describe the photographs. Compare them and answer the question: speculate (they might be…, perhaps she's hoping to…) and give your opinion.
Keep talking for the full minute. If you run out of things to say about one photograph, move to the other.

data.text: Part 1: talk about opinions, discussions and speaking up. Part 2: compare two photographs and say why the young people might want to make their voices heard.

activities.title: Reading and Use of English Part 7 — multiple matching. Which person…?

tips.expect: Five short texts, each by a different young writer, followed by ten questions in the form 'Which person…'. Letters can be used more than once, and there is no fixed order.
how: Read the questions first and underline the key idea in each one — they paraphrase the texts, so look for the same idea in different words, not matching vocabulary.
Read one whole text, then check it against every question before moving on to the next text — that is usually faster than reading all five texts first.
Be careful with texts that mention several ideas: the correct match is the person whose text really matches the exact meaning of the question, not just a shared topic.
tips.remember: There is no rule that each person is used the same number of times — check the whole text carefully before you decide.

data.title: Can our generation really change things?
data.intro: For the final unit, Miss Vega shared five posts from an international youth discussion forum, all answering the same question. Read what Amara, Lucas, Priya, Freya and Jack wrote, then answer the questions below.

sections.heading: Amara, 16, Ghana
sections.text: I used to think that changing the world meant marching in huge protests or making a speech that goes viral. Then our village started planting trees along the dry riverbed near my home, and within two years birds had come back that nobody remembered seeing. Nobody filmed it; nobody shared it online. What I have learned is that most real change happens quietly, on a small and local scale, long before anyone outside notices. Big campaigns matter, but they rarely succeed without hundreds of small, unnoticed efforts underneath them. So when people ask whether my generation can really change anything, I always point to the trees rather than to a hashtag.

sections.heading: Lucas, 17, Brazil
sections.text: Everyone in my class has shared a petition or reposted a cause at some point, and I did too, until I noticed how little actually followed. A post can reach thousands of people in an afternoon, yet the problem it complains about is often exactly the same a year later. I am not saying online action is worthless — it can spread information fast, and it helped organise a real clean-up event near my school last spring. My concern is that clicking a button feels so much like doing something that people stop there. Genuine change, I now believe, still needs the boring, offline part: meetings, paperwork, showing up.

sections.heading: Priya, 15, India
sections.text: My older cousins spent years studying for exams so they could eventually get an office job, and most of them are still waiting for one. I chose a different path: an apprenticeship with a local electrician. People sometimes look surprised when I say that fixing wiring is my contribution to changing things, but I disagree with them. Every village that gets reliable electricity for the first time changes because someone learned a practical trade well enough to install it properly. I think my generation talks a great deal about big ideas, and that is valuable, but the world is also changed, quietly, by people who know how to build and repair things.

sections.heading: Freya, 16, UK
sections.text: Before I joined my school's debating society, I assumed changing someone's mind meant winning an argument against them. I now think that is exactly backwards. The skill that actually changes things is listening well enough to understand why somebody disagrees with you in the first place, and then finding the one point where you might actually be right and they might be wrong. I have watched furious disagreements in our debate club end with both sides slightly closer to the middle, which never happens when people simply shout past each other. If my generation is going to change anything, I suspect it will be because we learned to disagree properly.

sections.heading: Jack, 17, Australia
sections.text: I joined our local council's youth board expecting fast results and left my first meeting rather deflated: three months of discussion over where to put a single new bicycle path. What I gradually understood, though, is that this slowness is not the same as failure. Real institutions move carefully because decisions affect people who were never in the room, and rushing them causes new problems. Two years later that bicycle path exists, and so does a youth curfew policy our board helped soften. Neither made the news. My generation is often told we are impatient, and perhaps we are, but I have learned that patience is itself a kind of power, if you are willing to use it.

activities.title: Language focus 1 — discourse markers for debating

data.title: Discourse markers for debating
data.can: I can use discourse markers to concede a point politely, weigh up both sides and sum up an argument in a debate.
data.intro: A good debate is not just about strong arguments — it's about handling disagreement with control. Discourse markers let you concede a point without losing your position, weigh two sides against each other, and sum up your view politely but firmly. Used naturally, they make you sound fluent and fair-minded, exactly what Speaking Part 4 and a good review reward.

examples.text: Having said that, I do think trades deserve more respect.
examples.note: concedes a previous point before disagreeing

examples.text: On balance, I'd say the arguments for university are slightly stronger.
examples.note: weighs up both sides before concluding

examples.text: All in all, it was a fair and well-argued debate.
To be honest, I hadn't considered that argument before.
The way I see it, both paths can lead to success.
That's a fair point, but it doesn't apply to every case.
examples.note: acknowledges the other person before disagreeing

rules: Use having said that / that said to accept a point and then add a contrast.
Use on balance and all in all to weigh arguments or summarise your overall opinion.
Use to be honest and the way I see it to introduce a personal opinion without sounding aggressive.
Use that's a fair point, but… to disagree respectfully instead of dismissing someone.
Put most of these markers at the start of the sentence, followed by a comma.
One or two markers per turn sound natural; using several in the same sentence sounds unnatural.

items.sentence: I understand your point. ___, I still think trades deserve more respect.
___, both sides had strong arguments today.
___, it was one of the best debates we've had this year.
___, I didn't expect Nadia's rebuttal to be so strong.
That's a fair point, ___ it doesn't change my overall opinion.
___, I think practical skills are just as valuable as academic ones.

activities.title: Reading and Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations

tips.expect: Six sentences, each followed by a second sentence with a gap and a key word. You complete the gap so that the second sentence means the same as the first, using between two and five words including the key word, which must not change.
how: Identify the structure being tested — this unit reviews mixed conditionals, the causative, relative clauses, persuasion verbs and debate vocabulary.
Write the whole gap, then read the complete second sentence in your head: does it mean exactly the same as the first?
Count your words carefully — contractions count as two words (didn't = did not).
tips.remember: Half marks exist: if the structure is right but a small word is wrong, you can still score one mark.

data.instructions: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first sentence, using the word given. Do not change the word given. You must use between two and five words, including the word given.

items.first: She didn't practise enough, so she isn't confident in the debate today.
items.second_end: more, she would be more confident in the debate today.

items.first: Mateo asked a technician to fix the microphone before the debate.
Nadia gave a rebuttal. It surprised everyone in the room.
The moderator said we should listen to each other more carefully.
In the end, Liam admitted that his argument was weaker than Sofía's.
We interviewed a student. Her speech had won the debate competition last year.
items.second_end: had won the debate competition last year.

activities.title: Listening Part 4 — multiple choice. Choose the best answer, A, B, C or D.

tips.expect: One interview of about three to four minutes with two speakers. You answer seven four-option questions about opinion, attitude, feeling and detail. You hear the recording twice.
how: Before listening, read all seven questions and options: they follow the order of the interview.
Listen for opinion and feeling words (surprised, relieved, confident, proud) as well as facts — several questions test attitude, not just information.
The wrong options are often almost true, or true about the wrong speaker — check exactly who says what.
tips.remember: Use the first listening to choose your best answer for every question; use the second listening only to check, not to start again.

data.voice_note: Presenter (Ryan) interviews Miss Vega, the students' English teacher, and Nadia, one of her Grade 10 students, about the final class debate.
data.script:
Presenter: Welcome back to Nordic Voices. Today we're talking about something a little different: a school debate that's been getting attention locally. With me are Miss Vega, who teaches English at the school, and Nadia, one of her Grade Ten students. Miss Vega, why a formal debate?
Miss Vega: Well, we'd spent the whole year building up to it, really. Every unit gave the students a piece of the puzzle, grammar, vocabulary, ways of arguing a point, and the debate was where all of that finally had somewhere to go. I could have set an essay instead, and it would have been easier to mark, frankly, but an essay doesn't teach you to think on your feet the way a live debate does.
Presenter: And Nadia, be honest, were you looking forward to it?
Nadia: Not even slightly. I'm usually the person who agrees with whoever spoke last, just to keep the peace. Standing up and defending one side of an argument, in front of the whole class, sounded like my idea of a nightmare.
Presenter: What changed?
Nadia: Practice, mostly. We did smaller debates for weeks before the big one, and I noticed that nobody actually remembered my mistakes the next day. That took the pressure off. By the time the real debate happened, I'd almost forgotten to be nervous.
Presenter: Miss Vega, was there a moment that surprised you?
Miss Vega: Honestly, yes, Nadia's rebuttal. She'd been fairly quiet in class discussions all year, so when she stood up and calmly took apart the other side's main point, in about thirty seconds, the whole room went silent. I don't think she realised how good it was until people started clapping.
Nadia: I still don't entirely believe that happened.
Presenter: What was the motion, exactly?
Miss Vega: That practical trades matter as much as university degrees. It ties into the project we've run all year, so it wasn't a random topic, the students had researched real examples, not just opinions.
Presenter: And did the debate change anyone's mind?
Nadia: A few people told me afterwards that they'd shifted slightly, which felt like a bigger achievement than winning would have been. Winning a vote doesn't prove your argument was right; changing someone's mind sort of does.
Presenter: That's a rather mature way of putting it.
Nadia: I'm quoting Miss Vega, to be honest.
Presenter: Miss Vega, what would you tell a teacher thinking about trying this with their own class?
Miss Vega: Build up to it slowly, and don't expect politeness to appear on its own, we spent real class time on how to disagree without being rude, and that paid off more than any grammar point did. Also, let the quiet students go last. They often surprise you.
Presenter: Nadia, one word for how you feel now that it's over?
Nadia: Relieved. And, oddly, a bit proud.
Presenter: Miss Vega, Nadia, thank you both very much.
Miss Vega: Thank you.
Nadia: Thanks for having us.

activities.title: Language focus 2 — grammar for a strong debate: mixed conditionals, the causative and relative clauses

data.title: Grammar for a strong debate: mixed conditionals, the causative and relative clauses
data.can: I can use mixed conditionals, the causative and relative clauses to build more sophisticated arguments in a debate.
data.intro: A great debate doesn't need new grammar — it needs this year's grammar working harder. Mixed conditionals let you connect a past cause to a present result, or a general truth to a past result; the causative lets you talk about arrangements without saying exactly who did the work; relative clauses let you add extra, precise information to a point without starting a new sentence. Use all three and your arguments will sound noticeably more mature.

examples.text: If we hadn't practised so much, we wouldn't be this confident today.
examples.note: mixed conditional: past condition, present result (Unit 1)

examples.text: If Liam weren't so calm under pressure, he wouldn't have won last year's debate.
examples.note: mixed conditional: general truth, past result (Unit 1)

examples.text: The school had a professional debate coach brought in before the final.
Nadia, whose rebuttal surprised everyone, is usually the quietest student in class.
examples.note: non-defining relative clause adds extra information (Unit 4)

examples.text: The motion, which had been chosen by the whole class, divided the room evenly.
examples.note: which refers back to the motion (Unit 4)

examples.text: We got the microphones tested the night before, which meant nothing went wrong.

rules: Mixed conditional 1: If + past perfect, would + infinitive, for a past cause with a present result: If she hadn't prepared, she wouldn't be so confident now.
Mixed conditional 2: If + past simple, would have + past participle, for an ongoing truth with a past result: If he weren't so shy, he wouldn't have avoided the debate last year.
Causative: have/get + object + past participle, for something done for you or arranged by you: We had the hall prepared. We got the posters printed.
Defining relative clauses (who, which, that, whose) identify which person or thing you mean, with no commas: the student who spoke last.
Non-defining relative clauses (who, which, whose, never that), with commas, add extra information that could be removed: Nadia, who is usually quiet, surprised everyone.
In debating language, one well-placed relative clause or mixed conditional makes a point sound more persuasive than three short simple sentences.

items.sentence: If we ___ so hard all year, we wouldn't be ready for today's debate.
If Liam ___ so nervous, he wouldn't have avoided speaking in public last year.
We ___ the sound system checked before the audience arrived.
The teacher ___ our essays corrected by a colleague this term.
Sofía, ___ argument was the strongest, spoke first.
The student ___ gave the final rebuttal is Nadia.

activities.title: Reading and Use of English Part 3 — word formation. Use the word given to form a word that fits the gap.

tips.expect: A short text (150–200 words) with eight gaps. Each gap has a base word in capitals at the end of the line; you write the correct form of that word — a noun, adjective, adverb, verb or negative form.
how: Decide what part of speech each gap needs by looking at the words around it: after a/an or the, you probably need a noun; before a noun, an adjective.
Check whether the meaning needs a negative form (un-, dis-, im-, in-) — the context often contains a clue such as 'surprisingly' or 'refreshingly'.
Read the whole sentence again once you've written your answer, to check spelling and that the word makes sense.
tips.remember: If your answer looks identical to the capitals, check it again — the base word is never the correct answer.

data.title: What the debate taught us
data.text: Learning to disagree well is one of the most useful skills a school debate can teach you, and this year's final project put that skill to the test. At the start of the year, open {1:DISAGREE} made most of the class feel rather uncomfortable, as if any argument might threaten a friendship. By the final unit, though, opinions were expressed with real {2:CONFIDENT}, and a lost vote no longer felt like a {3:PERSON} failure. Miss Vega's method was refreshingly {4:CONVENTION}: she gave less advice about facts than about tone, teaching phrases that combine {5:FIRM} with courtesy. What surprised everyone was that the loudest speaker at the start of the year often became the most {6:CONVINCE} by the end, having learned that {7:PATIENT} usually beats volume. The debate also revealed how {8:AWARE} some students had been of their own habit of interrupting, a habit almost nobody had noticed until it was pointed out. By the last week, the class agreed that the biggest lesson had nothing to do with grammar at all.

activities.title: Writing Part 2 — review. Plan, write 140–190 words and hand it in.

tips.expect: Writing Part 2: you choose one task from a choice of two or three, which may include a review. A review describes something (an event, a talk, a podcast) and gives your opinion of it, usually for a website or magazine. 140–190 words, semi-formal or neutral register.
how: Give the review a clear shape: what it was, what happened or what it covered, your opinion, and a recommendation.
Use discourse markers to organise your opinion (on balance, having said that, all in all) — reviews reward a controlled, balanced voice.
Support your opinion with a specific detail or example rather than only general praise or criticism.
tips.remember: A review needs a personal opinion and a recommendation — a text that only describes the event without saying what you thought of it will lose marks.

data.task:
You see this notice on your school's English-language website:

Reviews wanted!

Have you been to a debate, a talk or listened to a podcast recently? Write us a review saying what it was about, what you thought of the speakers, and whether you would recommend it to other students.

Write your review.
plan: Introduction: what you attended or listened to, and where and when.
Paragraph 2: what it was about and who took part — the topic and the speakers.
Paragraph 3: your opinion, using discourse markers to weigh strengths and weaknesses.
Conclusion: whether you would recommend it, and to whom.

Describing the event: It focused on the question of…
Recommending: I would definitely recommend it to…

checklist: I described the event and named the topic clearly.
I gave my opinion of the speakers or content, using discourse markers naturally.
I said whether I would recommend it, and to whom.
I used at least one mixed conditional, one causative form or one relative clause.
The register is appropriate for a school website: neutral and engaging, not overly formal.
data.model:
A model answer (151 words).

Last Friday I watched the final debate of our Inspiring Nordic project, held in the school hall in front of the whole of Grade Ten. The motion, which had been chosen by the class themselves, was that practical trades matter as much as university degrees.

Sofía opened confidently for the proposal, and Liam's replies were sharp and quick. The real surprise, though, was Nadia, whose calm rebuttal silenced the room completely — nobody expected the quietest student in the class to deliver the strongest argument of the afternoon. Mateo moderated fairly, giving both sides equal time.

On balance, I thought the proposal made the stronger case, mainly because their examples felt more concrete. Having said that, the opposing team's closing argument was genuinely persuasive, and the final vote was almost evenly split.

I would definitely recommend watching next year's debate, especially to anyone who thinks a school discussion can't be genuinely exciting.

activities.title: Speaking — Parts 3 and 4. Collaborative task and discussion. Record your best answer.

tips.expect: Part 3 (about 4 minutes): you and your partner discuss a question with five written prompts for about two minutes, then have one minute to reach a decision together. Part 4 (about 4 minutes): the examiner asks you both wider questions on the same theme.
how: In Part 3 you are not marked on agreeing with your partner; you are marked on interacting. Ask their opinion, respond to it, build on it, disagree politely.
Do not try to cover all five prompts. Two or three discussed properly is better than five rushed.
In the decision minute, negotiate: Shall we go for…? I'd be happy with that, as long as…
In Part 4, develop your answers: opinion, then reason, then example.
tips.remember: Look at your partner, not at the examiner. The examiner is listening, not talking.
